prompt: What does a reservation commit you to?
hint: Compare it with a savings plan's commitment.

choices.text: An amount of money per hour, spent on anything eligible
choices.why: That is a savings plan's commitment.

choices.text: One product, size and region, for one or three years
choices.why: Right. It discounts usage that matches what was bought.

choices.text: A minimum number of machines running at all times
choices.why: It commits to a kind of machine, not to keeping any running. Unused hours are still charged.

choices.text: A monthly budget that Azure enforces
choices.why: No budget is enforced by Azure, as lesson 13 showed.

prompt: A savings plan is committed to 10 an hour. In one hour the eligible usage comes to 6 at discounted prices. What happens to the other 4?
hint: Does an hour carry over?

choices.text: They carry over to the next hour
choices.why: Microsoft's documentation says the opposite: unused commitment for an hour expires.

choices.text: They are refunded at the end of the month
choices.why: A savings plan cannot be refunded at all, let alone hour by hour.

choices.text: They are applied to pay-as-you-go usage elsewhere
choices.why: The plan already covers all eligible usage in its scope; whatever it did not reach is billed normally.

choices.text: They are paid for and lost
choices.why: Right. Each hour stands alone, which is why a plan is sized to the spending present in every hour.

prompt: A machine costs an invented 1.00 an hour pay as you go and 0.60 an hour under a reservation. Above what percentage of the month must it run for the reservation to save money?
hint: The ratio of the two prices.

prompt: Why does `breakeven.py` multiply the commitment by all 730 hours but pay as you go only by the hours used?
hint: When is each one charged?

choices.text: A commitment is charged every hour of its term
choices.why: Right. Pay as you go stops when the machine stops; the reservation does not.

choices.text: Reservations bill a whole month in advance
choices.why: Up front or monthly, the total is the same; the point is that unused hours are paid.

choices.text: Pay as you go is billed per second, so its hours are fewer
choices.why: Per-second billing changes the granularity, not the fact that idle time costs nothing.

choices.text: The program assumes the reserved machine never stops
choices.why: It assumes nothing about the machine; it charges the reservation whatever the machine does.

prompt: The shop's daily compute spending, at discounted prices, is never below 8 an hour and averages 15. A colleague proposes a savings plan of 15 an hour. What is wrong with the number?
hint: What happens in the quiet hours?

choices.text: Nothing: a plan should match the average
choices.why: The average includes the quiet hours, and in those the plan's unused part is lost.

choices.text: Savings plans must be a round multiple of 10
choices.why: No such rule; the amount is yours to choose.

choices.text: In every hour below 15, part of it is paid for nothing
choices.why: Right. Sized to the spending present in every hour, near 8, nothing is wasted.

choices.text: It should be a reservation, since the usage is steady
choices.why: Usage that moves between 8 and much more is exactly what a reservation fits badly.

prompt: Put Microsoft's sequence for saving on compute in order.
hint: Waste goes first; flexibility last.
items: remove what is unused and resize what is too large
reserve what runs all the time and will not change
cover the steady part of what moves with a savings plan
leave the rest on pay as you go
trap: Buying a discount before removing waste only makes the waste cheaper.

prompt: Which of these can be done with a savings plan bought last month?
hint: Compare its cancellation policy with a reservation's.

choices.text: Return it for a refund up to USD 50,000 a year
choices.why: That limit is for reservations. Savings plans cannot be cancelled or refunded.

choices.text: Cancel it, paying a fee
choices.why: There is no cancellation with or without a fee.

choices.text: Exchange it for a reservation of the same value
choices.why: The trade goes the other way: reservations can be traded in for a savings plan.

choices.text: Let it apply across regions and machine sizes
choices.why: Right. That flexibility is what it offers in place of a deeper discount.

prompt: Azure's price calculator counts a month as ___ hours.
hint: 8,760 divided by twelve.

prompt: What does Azure Hybrid Benefit remove from a Windows virtual machine's price?
hint: The price has two parts.

choices.text: The cost of the disk
choices.why: Disks are billed apart and the benefit does not touch them.

choices.text: The compute part, leaving only the licence
choices.why: It is the other way round: you bring the licence, Azure still charges the machine.

choices.text: The Windows licence part
choices.why: Right. The machine is billed at the base compute rate.

choices.text: Everything, for up to 180 days
choices.why: The 180 days are dual use of a licence during a migration, not a free period.

prompt: Who checks that a machine marked `licenseType: 'Windows_Server'` is really covered by a licence?
hint: Is it checked when the machine is created?

choices.text: Azure, when the machine is created
choices.why: Azure takes the flag as your statement and checks nothing.

choices.text: Nobody at the time; an audit, later
choices.why: Right. Which is why the asset team has to agree with the count of flags.

choices.text: The Bicep compiler, against the tenant's licences
choices.why: The compiler did not even notice `Windows_Sever`.

choices.text: Microsoft, by reading the machine's disk
choices.why: Nothing is read from the machine to decide the price.

prompt: `vm.bicep` compiled with no network interface and no disk. What does that show?
hint: What did lesson 1 say compiling is?

choices.text: That the type does not require them, and Azure checks the rest
choices.why: Right. A fragment that compiles is a fragment.

choices.text: That Azure creates them automatically
choices.why: Nothing says so; Resource Manager would refuse a machine without them.

choices.text: That the Hybrid Benefit makes them unnecessary
choices.why: The benefit is about the licence price only.

choices.text: That Bicep fills in defaults from the tenant
choices.why: Bicep knows nothing about the tenant at build time.

prompt: Cost analysis shows a Windows licence meter on three machines the company believes are under Hybrid Benefit. What does each of those lines mean?
hint: How does the benefit show on the bill?

choices.text: A charge for something already paid for
choices.why: Right. The flag is missing, perhaps lost in a redeployment.

choices.text: The machines are using more licences than allowed
choices.why: That is the opposite problem: too many flags. Here a flag is missing.

choices.text: The benefit is applied and the meter is informational
choices.why: Under the benefit, the licence meter is absent. Its presence is the charge.

choices.text: Azure rejected the licence after an audit
choices.why: Azure checks no licence and does not reject one.

prompt: On a virtual machine, the Hybrid Benefit is the property `___`.
hint: Its value in the lesson is `Windows_Server`.

prompt: In a FOCUS export, which column holds what a line adds to the invoice on the day it was charged?
hint: Lesson 13's actual cost.

choices.text: `EffectiveCost`
choices.why: That is the amortised cost, spread over the usage it covered.

choices.text: `PricingCategory`
choices.why: That says which kind of price applied, not how much.

choices.text: `BilledCost`
choices.why: Right. The actual cost, as a column.

choices.text: `ChargeFrequency`
choices.why: That says how often a charge occurs.

prompt: On the day an up-front reservation is bought, what do the lines for the machines it covers show?
hint: Where did the money already go?

choices.text: `Standard` usage at pay-as-you-go prices
choices.why: They are covered, so their pricing category is `Committed`.

choices.text: `Committed` usage with a billed cost of zero
choices.why: Right. The money is on the `Purchase` line; their effective cost carries a daily share.

choices.text: Nothing, until the reservation's first month ends
choices.why: Usage lines appear every day the machines run.

choices.text: A `Credit` that cancels their usage
choices.why: A reservation is not a credit; its effect is the pricing category.

prompt: From one month to the next, a machine's usage hours stayed the same and its cost rose. Its lines moved from `Committed` to `Standard`. What is the likeliest explanation?
hint: Nothing new was created.

choices.text: Microsoft raised its pay-as-you-go price
choices.why: A price rise would leave the pricing category unchanged.

choices.text: The machine was counted twice
choices.why: The hours stayed the same; nothing doubled.

choices.text: A tax was added to the subscription
choices.why: Tax arrives as `Tax` lines, not as a change in the usage lines' category.

choices.text: A commitment stopped applying to it
choices.why: Right: a reservation expired, or the machine was resized out of its size family.

prompt: A pay-as-you-go subscription's invoice and cost analysis's month disagree. What does the lesson name first?
hint: Which month does each one show?

choices.text: The invoice is rounded to whole dollars
choices.why: No such rounding explains a difference of days.

choices.text: Cost analysis leaves out reservations
choices.why: It shows them, in actual or amortised form.

choices.text: The invoice covers a billing period, not the calendar month
choices.why: Right. Both totals can be right.

choices.text: One of the two is wrong and needs a support request
choices.why: Compare like with like before concluding anything is wrong.

prompt: Match each FOCUS column to the question it answers.
hint: Two of them are costs, measured differently.

pairs.right: is it usage, a purchase, tax, a credit or an adjustment?
what is the line's amortised share?
is it a correction to an earlier period?

prompt: A team buys a one-year reservation for its staging machine, which runs only during office hours, about 30% of the month. Using the lesson's invented prices (1.00 and 0.60), what happens?
hint: Where is the break-even?

choices.text: It saves 40% as promised
choices.why: The discount is per hour; an hour bought and not used saves nothing.

choices.text: Azure refuses a reservation for a machine that stops
choices.why: Azure sells it; the arithmetic is yours to do.

choices.text: It costs the same, since the reservation stops with the machine
choices.why: A reservation is charged every hour of its term.

choices.text: It costs more than pay as you go would have
choices.why: Right. 30% is below the 60% break-even.

prompt: Which of these can make a bill rise with no new resource created? Choose all that apply.
hint: The section listed four surprises.

choices.text: A reservation expiring
choices.why: Right. Its usage moves to `Standard`.

choices.text: A machine losing its `licenseType` in a redeployment
choices.why: Right. A licence meter appears.

choices.text: Switching cost analysis to amortised cost
choices.why: A view changes how a cost is drawn, not what is billed.

choices.text: An up-front savings plan purchase
choices.why: Right. A `Purchase` line in `BilledCost`.

choices.text: A budget alert being sent
choices.why: Alerts cost nothing and change nothing.

prompt: Why does the course refuse to quote a real price for a reservation, even approximately?
hint: Where must a price come from, and with what beside it?

choices.text: Reservations have no public price
choices.why: They do: the Retail Prices API lists them under `Reservation`.

choices.text: No price list was reachable, and a price needs its source and date
choices.why: Right. A number nobody read from the list would be invented.

choices.text: Prices are confidential to each customer
choices.why: The retail prices are published for anybody.

choices.text: Reservations are priced only in US dollars
choices.why: The currency is not the reason; the source is.
